subject: Lande et al. (1982)
object: Lande et al. (1982) studied erythrocyte membrane proteins from 2 patients with congenital hemolytic anemia caused by increased erythrocyte membrane permeability to Na and K: one had hereditary stomatocytosis and one had cryohydrocytosis. On one-dimensional SDS gel electrophoresis, the 28,000-dalton band 7 component was reduced in both patients. On two-dimensional electrophoresis, this component resolved into 2 proteins, 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. Protein 22 x 8 was completely absent in both patients, while 60 x 8 was present.

subject: Lande et al. (1982)
object: Lande et al. (1982) found that all band 7 proteins, including 22 x 8, were present in every normal subject and reticulocytosis control they surveyed. Because the missing protein was unique to the patients, the authors raised the possibility that absence of this band 7 protein is responsible for the increased Na and K permeability in hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis.

subject: Fricke et al. (2004)
object: Fricke et al. (2004) described 2 patients with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. In both, the passive red cell K+ leak was lowest at around 20 to 25 degrees C, so the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C. Both had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly. The authors suggested that this probably defined a new haemato-neurological syndrome.

subject: Fricke et al. (2004)
object: Fricke et al. (2004) described 3 new isolated cases and 1 new pedigree of hereditary stomatocytosis, and gave further details on 1 previously reported case. In every case, Western blotting of red cell membranes showed a deficiency of stomatin, the 32-kD membrane protein. All cases had pronounced cation leaks at 37 degrees C, with markedly abnormal intracellular Na+ and K+ concentrations. Immunocytochemistry showed that the stomatin deficiency was not complete: some red cells were stomatin positive, and all platelets and neutrophils were stomatin positive.

subject: Fricke et al. (2004)
object: Fricke et al. (2004) found that the stomatin-deficient cases differed markedly in how the passive K+ leak depended on temperature. Three cases showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence. The other 2 had a minimum at 20 to 25 degrees C, which is the cryohydrocytosis phenotype.

subject: Flatt et al. (2011)
object: Flatt et al. (2011) noted that they had previously reported 2 cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis (sdCHC), a rare form of stomatocytosis associated with a cold-induced cation leak, hemolytic anemia, and hepatosplenomegaly, as well as cataracts, seizures, mental retardation, and movement disorder.

subject: Flatt et al. (2011)
object: In the 2 patients with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis, Flatt et al. (2011) identified 2 different mutations in the SLC2A1 gene. Expression studies in Xenopus oocytes showed that the mutations caused both loss of glucose transport and a cation leak. On the basis of a 3-dimensional model of GLUT1, the authors proposed potential mechanisms underlying the phenotypes of the 2 mutations.

subject: Flatt et al. (2011)
object: Flatt et al. (2011) found that loss of stomatin during erythropoiesis in sdCHC occurs during reticulocyte maturation and involves endocytosis.

subject: Bawazir et al. (2012)
object: Bawazir et al. (2012) described an infant with GLUT1 deficiency and a cation-leaky red cell state who presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction, and microcephaly. Later, seizures occurred and developmental milestones were delayed. Brain MRI and CT showed multiple abnormalities, including periventricular calcification, and visual impairment resulted from cataracts and retinal dysfunction.

subject: Bawazir et al. (2012)
object: Bawazir et al. (2012) found that the patient's red cells were extremely leaky to cations, which caused the hemolysis. Red cells lost potassium in a temperature-dependent way, which explained the hyperkalemia as pseudohyperkalemia.

subject: Bawazir et al. (2012)
object: In the proband, Bawazir et al. (2012) identified a trinucleotide deletion in the SLC2A1 gene that deletes isoleucine 435 or 436 of GLUT1. They noted that this was the fourth pedigree reported with this syndrome.

subject: SLC2A1 trinucleotide deletion coding for the deletion of isoleucine 435 or 436
Bawazir et al. (2012)
object: Bawazir et al. (2012) suggested that the multisystem pathology probably reflects two effects: deficient glucose transport at the blood-brain barrier, as in typical GLUT1 deficiency, and the harmful osmotic effects of a cation-leaky membrane protein in cells that express GLUT1, notably red cells.

subject: STOMATIN-DEFICIENT CRYOHYDROCYTOSIS WITH NEUROLOGIC DEFECTS
